claims.proposition_evaluated: Edmonton's automated counters recorded nearly 1.3 million cycling trips in the first seven months of 2026 - operationalised as the sum of total_cyclist_count in the City of Edmonton dataset 'Bike and Pedestrian Counts (Eco Counter)' (tq23-qn4m) for log timestamps from 2026-01-01 through 2026-07-31 inclusive, across every counter published in that window.
claims.interpretation_notes: I queried tq23-qn4m directly through the City's Socrata API on 2026-09-03. The published window is complete: the maximum log timestamp inside the period is 2026-07-31 23:45, and the dataset extends to 2026-09-02 23:45, so the brief's short-window rule (return Not established) is not triggered. Network total = 1,291,714. That falls inside the primary Supported band (at least 1.10 million and below 1.50 million) and also inside the alternative Supported band (at least 1.17 million and below 1.43 million). Both cutoff sets return Supported. The City's own word is 'count', not 'trip': the dataset is titled 'Bike and Pedestrian Counts', the field is 'Total Cyclist Count', and the City's description says the data is raw and has not been through quality control or quality assurance. The holder's word 'trips' is the word CBC used, not the word the City uses, and the figure is a count of passages past fixed points. I used only the base counts dataset tq23-qn4m for the total, and the locations dataset py7x-4d39 and the Bike Routes dataset vd4b-a4iv for the on-street/off-street split. A derived view, 'Daily Pedestrian and Bike Counts' (sw7k-ptx8), exists on the same portal; I did not rely on it.

supporting_evidence.finding: Sum of total_cyclist_count for log_timestamp from 2026-01-01T00:00:00 to 2026-07-31T23:45:00 = 1,291,714, over 933,576 fifteen-minute records at 48 distinct counter locations. Query run 2026-09-03 against the Socrata endpoint https://data.edmonton.ca/resource/tq23-qn4m.json with $select=sum(total_cyclist_count) and the date range in $where. 41 of the 48 locations recorded a non-zero cyclist count; the other 7 are pedestrian-configured.

challenging_evidence.finding: The same window in the two preceding years is larger, not smaller: 2025-01-01 to 2025-07-31 = 1,611,749 (49 counter locations); 2024-01-01 to 2024-07-31 = 1,547,532 (50 locations). The 2026 figure is 19.9 percent below the 2025 same-window figure (my calculation: (1,291,714 - 1,611,749) / 1,611,749). The decline is spread across most counters and is very large at a few - 102 Avenue E of 105 Street fell from 83,723 to 20,609 with a full 212 days of records in both years. This does not bear on whether the stated figure is right, but it does contradict any reading of the figure as evidence of continuing growth.

limitations: Shared dataset: the Eco-Counter counts dataset tq23-qn4m serves both claim 1 (a seven-month network total) and claim 2 (per-corridor July daily medians). A network total says nothing about any one corridor and a corridor rate says nothing about the network.

A counter records a passage past a fixed point. It is not a person and it is not a journey. One person riding to work and home past the same counter is two counts; one journey past two counters is two counts; a person riding where there is no counter is none. The number of distinct people behind 1,291,714 is unknown and no counter can establish it.

The City labels the data raw and not quality-assured. The City has acknowledged one specific error, pedestrian and cyclist counts switched at three sites for 2021 and 2022, which it said affects historical data prior to 2023 only. I have not independently verified that no error affects 2026.

Coverage is uneven across the window. Of the 48 locations reporting, 41 have all 212 days; the exceptions are Terwillegar Park Footbridge (141 days), Funicular @ 100 St (171), Whitemud Ravine Boardwalk (165), 103 Street N of 100 Avenue (131), 103 Street N of 102 Avenue (86), Gold Bar Trail (202), 102A Avenue W of 96 Street (205). Network wide there are 20,348 distinct fifteen-minute stamps against a theoretical 20,352 (212 days x 96), the four missing being the spring daylight-saving hour. Missing days can only add to the total, and adding them would not move the figure out of the Supported band unless they added more than 208,000 counts.

The 48 counters are not a fixed panel: locations are added and retired. Four new counters (100 Street S of 81 Avenue, 106 Street S of 61 Avenue W, 142 Street N of Whitemud Drive, 23 Avenue W of Hewes Way) first report on 2026-08-30, after the window, and 106 Street N of Jasper Avenue stopped on 2025-07-16 and contributes nothing to 2026.

I did not find the City itself publishing this seven-month total. The City publishes an open-data story, 'Cycling in Edmonton' (https://data.edmonton.ca/stories/s/Cycling-in-Edmonton/ktwr-rn4x/), but the page I retrieved returned only portal navigation, so I cannot say what figures it prints. The 1.3 million figure in circulation traces to CBC's analysis, not to a City publication.
unknowns: How many distinct people the 1,291,714 counts represent. No published instrument answers this.

Whether the 19.9 percent year-over-year fall in the same window is real cycling behaviour, a device or siting change, construction on measured corridors, or a data-processing artefact. The City has not published an explanation.
Whether the City applied its own gap-filling or correction to the 2026 records between the CBC analysis of 2026-07-31 and my pull of 2026-09-03. The dataset carries no revision history.
Whether any counters were physically moved during the window. The dataset publishes coordinates but no installation or relocation log.

claims.suggested_one_line: Edmonton's automated counters recorded 1,291,714 bicycle counts between 1 January and 31 July 2026 - the 'nearly 1.3 million' figure checks out, though the City calls them counts, not trips, and the same window in 2025 was higher.
claims.suggested_short_answer: The number is right. Summing the City's Eco-Counter open data for 1 January to 31 July 2026 gives 1,291,714 bicycle counts across 48 counter locations. But the City's word is 'count', not 'trip': a counter records a passage past a fixed point, so a return commute past one counter is two, and how many distinct people are behind the figure is unknown. Two things sit beside it. The City labels the data raw and not quality-assured. And the same seven months in 2025 recorded 1,611,749 - about 20 percent more.

claims.proposition_evaluated: The Edmonton bike lanes that are metered, including the lanes residents named as empty, carry little or no bicycle traffic - operationalised as: every City automated bicycle counter in the verdict set defined by the brief's five membership tests has a July 2025 median daily bicycle count below 25 (alternative cutoff 50).
claims.interpretation_notes: I ran the five tests from published fields alone, in order, against tq23-qn4m (counts, coordinates and service), py7x-4d39 (locations) and vd4b-a4iv (Bike Routes), all pulled 2026-09-03. TEST 1, universe: 51 distinct counter_location_description values whose counter_configuration names cyclists or bikes. 10 pedestrian-only locations removed: Capilano Bridge, Emily Murphy, Funicular @ 100 St, Hermitage South, Keillor Point, Keillor Point (EBD into Keillor Point/WBD out of Keillor Point), Queen Elizabeth Park 2, Riverside Golf Course, Sir Wilfrid Laurier Park, Whitemud Ravine Boardwalk. TEST 2, in service on 2025-07-01: 42 pass, 9 removed - 100 Street S of 81 Avenue, 106 Street S of 61 Avenue W, 142 Street N of Whitemud Drive and 23 Avenue W of Hewes Way (first record 2026-08-30, after the date); 105 Avenue W of 101 Street (last record 2023-03-19); 105 Avenue W of 109 Street (2021-07-04); 99 Street N of 102A Avenue (2024-04-03); Rossdale SUP (2024-04-24); Woodward Trail / Wolf Willow EBD/WBD (2022-12-31). TEST 3, on-street or off-street, by nearest built Bike Routes segment to the counter's published coordinates: 21 on-street, 21 off-street, 0 unclassifiable. Every counter had a segment within 30 m and no ON ROAD/OFF ROAD tie within 0.1 m; the closest call was 96 Street S of Jasper Ave at ON 6.7 m against OFF 55.2 m. No counter is borderline under the ten-metre rule: the smallest gap between nearest ON ROAD and nearest OFF ROAD across all 42 candidates is 20.8 m (High Level Bridge East). The 21 removed as off-street, with distance to the nearest OFF ROAD segment and its classification: 102 Avenue SUP W Groat Rd Bridge (0.3 m, Shared Pathway), 121 Street SUP N of 107 Avenue (3.2, Shared Pathway), 163 Ave SUP W 75 Street (2.6, Shared Pathway), 91 Street S Whitemud Dr (18.5, Shared Pathway), Belgravia Rd Foot Bridge SUP (0.5, Shared Pathway), Buena Vista Bridge (3.4, Shared Trail), Capilano SUP (1.7, Shared Pathway), East Trails (0.7, Shared Pathway), Gold Bar Trail (4.3, Shared Pathway), Hermitage North (0.8, Shared Pathway), High Level Bridge East (1.9, Shared Pathway), High Level Bridge West (3.3, Shared Pathway), LRT SUP East of 92 Street (1.1, Shared Pathway), MacKinnon Ravine (2.2, Shared Pathway), Power Line Tr E Carter Crest Way (0.9, Shared Pathway), Queen Elizabeth Park (0.8, Shared Pathway), Railtown Park SUP (1.2, Shared Pathway), Terwillegar Park Footbridge (1.2, Shared Pathway), Victoria Trail S 137 Avenue (2.2, Shared Pathway), Wedgewood (8.5, Shared Pathway), Woodward Trail Wolf Willow (0.3, Shared Trail). TEST 4, out of service: one counter leaves the set - 106 Street N of Jasper Avenue, last record anywhere 2025-07-16, so it stopped inside the measured month and never resumed. Its last stable level is a median of 177.5 bicycles/day in June 2025, the last calendar month it published in full (30 of 30 days). It was on a Protected Bike Lane 2.5 m from its coordinates. Removing it does not help the claim: it was carrying roughly seven times the primary cutoff while it worked. TEST 5, measured: all 20 remaining counters published bicycle counts on all 31 days of July 2025. None is under-reported. The verdict set is non-empty, nothing is unclassifiable, nothing is under-reported, so the cutoffs apply. RESULT. Every one of the 20 July medians is at or above 25, the lowest being 46. Under the primary cutoff no counter is below it, so the verdict is Contradicted. Under the alternative cutoff of 50 a day, one counter (96 Street S of Jasper Ave, median 46) is below and 19 are at or above, which returns Partially supported. The finding is therefore definition-sensitive at the alternative cutoff, and the story should say so beside the verdict. The verdict I report is the primary one. This finding covers the lanes the City counts and no others. The counters sit where the City chose to monitor; they are not a random or representative sample of Edmonton's on-street bike lanes, and nobody publishes a representative sample of them. A holder who means every lane in the city has not been answered.

supporting_evidence.finding: The lowest July 2025 median in the verdict set, 96 Street S of Jasper Ave at 46 bicycles/day, is the only counter that falls below the alternative cutoff of 50. It is also the only one that could be described as quiet relative to the rest: its 2025 calendar-year total is 8,661 against 200,981 at 83 Avenue W of 99 Street. Under the alternative cutoff the verdict would be Partially supported rather than Contradicted, which is the one respect in which the holders' statement survives contact with the meters.

limitations: Shared dataset: the Eco-Counter counts dataset tq23-qn4m serves both claim 1 (a seven-month network total) and claim 2 (per-corridor July daily medians). A network total says nothing about any one corridor and a corridor rate says nothing about the network.

The verdict covers the 20 on-street lanes the City meters and kept in service through July 2025. It covers no other lane. The counters sit at monitoring locations the City chose, they are not a sample of the network, and no representative sample of Edmonton's on-street bike lanes is published. The unmetered lanes were not measured and nobody publishes a measure of them.

Definition-sensitive. Primary cutoff of 25 a day returns Contradicted (0 of 20 below). Alternative cutoff of 50 a day returns Partially supported (1 of 20 below: 96 Street S of Jasper Ave at 46). Neither figure comes from a pre-existing standard.

Three counters in the verdict set have partial 2025 records, so their calendar-year totals are not comparable with the others: 132 Ave E of 108 St N and S first report 2025-06-16 (199 days, no January figure); 103 Street N of 102 Avenue records 2025-05-02 to 2025-12-19 (232 days, no January figure); 119 Ave E 91 Street evo has a gap from 2025-01-22 to 2025-05-01 (265 days). Every one of them still has all 31 days of July 2025, which is what the verdict turns on.

One counter left the set under test 4: 106 Street N of Jasper Avenue, last record 2025-07-16, last stable level median 177.5 bicycles/day in June 2025. A verdict computed over a set that lost a counter has to say which counter it lost, and this is it.

The July median is a summer measure, chosen by the brief to test the claim at its strongest for the lanes. The January 2025 medians in the same set run from no data to 212 a day, and several are in single figures - 119 Avenue at 6, 76 Avenue at 9 and 14, 96 Street at 9. A holder arguing about winter is arguing about a different number, and that number is not what this verdict tests.
The data is raw and not quality-assured, by the City's own description.

claims.proposition_evaluated: Most cycling in Edmonton is recreational rather than commuting - operationalised as bicycle trips classified as recreation, exercise or leisure, as a share of all bicycle trips, from the most recent Edmonton region household travel survey published by 2026-09-03.
claims.interpretation_notes: Source and categories. The 2015 Edmonton and Region Household Travel Survey publishes trip purpose crossed with mode in Table 3-10. Its purpose categories, verbatim: HB-Work, HB-PSE (home-based post-secondary education), HB-School, HB-Shopping, HB-Social / Rec, HB-Personal Bus., HB-Pick up/Drop off, HB-Other, NHB-Work, NHB-Other (HB is home-based, NHB non-home-based). My mapping, stated before the figures: recreational = HB-Social / Rec; commuting = HB-Work plus NHB-Work; everything else is a third category and belongs to neither. The brief's Contradicted branch explicitly contemplates 'some third purpose category', so a complete binary mapping is not required and the Not established branch is not triggered by the presence of school, shopping and errand trips. Arithmetic, labelled as my calculation. The survey publishes bicycle as a share within each purpose, not purpose within bicycle, so I multiplied each purpose total by its published whole-percent bicycle share for City of Edmonton residents: HB-Work 650,700 x 3% = 19,521; HB-PSE 82,500 x 3% = 2,475; HB-School 255,400 x 2% = 5,108; HB-Shopping 352,600 x 1% = 3,526; HB-Social/Rec 399,800 x 3% = 11,994; HB-Personal Bus. 226,200 x 1% = 2,262; HB-Pick up/Drop off 217,000 x 1% = 2,170; HB-Other 172,100 x 1% = 1,721; NHB-Work 185,800 x 1% = 1,858; NHB-Other 597,000 x 1% = 5,970. Sum 56,605, against the 54,800 bicycle trips the survey publishes in Table 3-2 - 3.3 percent over, which is the rounding. Recreational share = 11,994 / 56,605 = 21.2 percent (21.9 percent on the published 54,800 denominator). Commuting share = 21,379 / 56,605 = 37.8 percent. HB-Work alone is 34.5 percent and is the largest single category. Verdict. Commuting exceeds recreation and recreation is at most 35 percent, so the primary ladder returns Contradicted. The alternative ladder (Supported above 45 percent; Partially supported above 30 percent, at most 45, and largest) also returns Contradicted, since 21 percent is neither above 30 nor the largest category. Both cutoff sets agree. Rounding sensitivity. The published shares are whole percentages, so I tested the extremes. Even with HB-Social/Rec at the top of its rounding band (3.5 percent, 13,993 trips) and HB-Work at the bottom of its (2.5 percent, 16,268) plus NHB-Work at 0.5 percent (929), commuting at 17,197 still exceeds recreation at 13,993, and recreation is 25.5 percent of the published bicycle total. The verdict does not turn on the rounding.

supporting_evidence.finding: Two Edmonton sources point the other way and are worth stating because they are what a holder of this claim would reach for. The City's August 2014 bike ridership survey asked riders why they ride, multi-select: of 482 respondents who answered, 87.3 percent ticked recreation or leisure enjoyment, 47.5 percent transportation trips, 42.1 percent commuting to work or school and 19.9 percent other reasons. This is an opt-in panel, the answers are reasons rather than trips, and the percentages sum well past 100 because people ticked more than one, so it cannot carry the verdict. But it does show most riders in that sample ride for recreation at least sometimes, which is a different proposition from most cycling being recreational.

limitations: Shared document: the 2015 Edmonton and Region Household Travel Survey Summary Report (City of Edmonton, published April 2018) is the source for both claim 5 and claim 8. Claim 5 takes Table 3-2/Figure 3-4 (bicycle trips as a share of all trips). Claim 8 takes Table 3-10 (trip purpose by mode). Two findings from one document, not two independent findings.

This is the weakest finding in the set and the confidence is Low for two reasons that both cut the same way. First, the 2015 survey is a weekday travel diary. Weekend travel is absent from it entirely, and weekend riding is where recreational cycling concentrates, so a weekday-only instrument will understate the recreational share of cycling as a whole. No full-week Edmonton instrument exists, so this is a limit of the record rather than a choice, but a reader should not take 21 percent as the recreational share of all Edmonton cycling. Second, the survey does not publish the purpose breakdown of bicycle trips at all; I derived it from a cross-tabulation whose bicycle cells are rounded to whole percentages. The direction survives the rounding, but the precision does not.

The survey does not publish the sample size for bicycle trips specifically. With 1.7 percent of trips by bicycle in a sample of about 15,300 City households, the bicycle cells in a ten-column purpose table rest on small numbers, and the summary report gives no sampling error for them.
The figure is eleven years old on the as-of date. Fieldwork was autumn 2015 - and an autumn diary is itself a seasonal slice, since Edmonton cycling peaks in July.

Purpose mix for all modes, for comparison, from Table 3-9 (weekday, City residents, 2015): HB-Work 21 percent, HB-Social / Recreation 13 percent, HB-Shopping 11 percent, HB-School 8 percent, NHB-Other 19 percent. Cycling's mix is more work-weighted and more recreation-weighted than the all-mode mix, at the expense of shopping and errands.

Trip purpose and rider type are different things. A finding that most bicycle trips are for commuting does not mean most people who ride are commuters, and the 2014 panel's 87 percent who ride for recreation at least sometimes is consistent with both.
